scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is named for James Hay, 15th Earl of Erroll.
While Francis Peacock dedicated music to the Earl in 1805, the choreography is not found in his writings.
The primary historical source is the Frederick Hill Manuscript of 1841.
on_screen: Map: Scotland · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a staple of the Scottish National dance competitive repertoire.
It represents the refined, 'step' tradition of Scottish movement, often associated with the dancing masters of the 19th century and the social elite of the North East.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: It is a solo Scottish national dance characterized by a soft, balletic style.
Dancers perform intricate footwork that requires high technical proficiency and balance.
While originally a hard-sole dance, it is now performed in soft shoes.
Watch for Step dancing.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to two specific slow reels in 4/4 time: 'Earl of Erroll' and 'The 23rd Countess of Erroll'.
The music is typically provided by a solo piper or a fiddler at Highland games.
Listen for the Bagpipes, Fiddle.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 100 beats a minute.
A measured 4/4 reel rhythm played with the clarity required for step dancing. The melody is formal and repetitive, providing a steady pulse for the dancer's weight changes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: James Hay (15th Earl of Erroll), Francis Peacock (18th-century dancing master), Frederick Hill (author of the 1841 manuscript), and Isobel 'Tibbie' Cramb (20th-century dance scholar).
A distinct 'Earl of Errol's Reel' exists in the Scottish country dance repertoire (a 6/8 jig for six dancers), but it is a separate tradition from this solo national dance.
The dance belongs to the Scottish National dance family, descending from 19th-century step dancing traditions and preserved through the Hill Manuscript (1841).
